analysis.one_liner: Phases out the federal estate and gift tax over ten years, repealing it entirely in 2010.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 279-136 and the Senate 59-39, but President Clinton vetoed it on August 31, 2000, and the House's override attempt failed 274-157, well short of the two-thirds needed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would gradually lower the estate tax rate, raise the exemption from $675,000 to $1 million, and repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes outright for deaths after 2009. In exchange, it would end the 'step-up in basis' rule, meaning heirs would owe capital gains tax on appreciation in inherited property above certain thresholds. Only estates above the exemption owed the tax at all, so the benefits would flow overwhelmingly to the heirs of the wealthiest households, while the lost federal revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. At the time, the estate tax applied only to estates above $675,000 (rising to $1 million under the bill), so roughly the top few percent of estates owed anything, and the biggest savings went to estates worth many millions. Family-owned farms and small businesses also gained, though most already fell below the exemption.

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the unified credit with a rising exemption ($675,000 in 2001, $700,000 in 2002-03, $850,000 in 2004, $950,000 in 2005, $1 million from 2006 on) and cuts the top rate from 55% toward 50% before full repeal [S4].
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes are repealed for deaths and transfers after December 31, 2009 [S3][S4].

The bill expands the estate tax exclusion for land placed under conservation easements, extending eligibility to easements within 50 miles of a metropolitan area or national park and 25 miles of an urban national forest [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall by tens of billions over the phase-out, which other taxpayers or government programs would absorb. Heirs would also take on new recordkeeping and capital gains exposure under the carryover basis rules, which exempt only the first $1.3 million of inherited property (plus up to $3 million more for a surviving spouse) [S4].

drawbacks.text: Because the tax already exempted estates up to the rising exemption, the overwhelming share of the revenue lost would have gone to the largest estates, not to ordinary families [S4].

Ending the step-up in basis means heirs above the $1.3 million/$3 million thresholds would owe capital gains on inherited appreciation and would need cost records for inherited property, a real burden for executors and families [S4].
Repeal would remove a tax that currently rewards charitable bequests, and the revenue loss would put pressure on other taxes or spending [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered real, large tax cuts, but concentrated them on the estates that owed the tax — by definition the wealthiest few percent — while the revenue cost was spread across everyone. The carryover basis offset eased the fiscal cost but shifted new tax-compliance work onto heirs, including modest ones above the thresholds. As a piece of tax policy it was a straightforward transfer to concentrated wealth with a partially offsetting complication for everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: President Clinton vetoed the bill, and when the House tried to override, it got 274 votes where 290 were needed, so the veto stood and the bill went back to committee as the Congress wound down.

narrative.text: The Ways and Means Committee reported the bill 24-11 on May 25, 2000, and the House passed it 279-136 on June 9, with 213 of 222 Republicans in favor and 65 of 211 Democrats crossing over [S6][S8].
The Senate cleared the way with a 99-1 vote to proceed on July 11, then passed the bill without amendment 59-39 on July 14, with 50 of 55 Republicans and 9 of 45 Democrats in favor [S9][S11][S6].
The President vetoed it on August 31, 2000 [S6].
The House override vote on September 7 failed 274-157, short of the two-thirds majority required; 220 of 223 Republicans voted to override but only 53 of 210 Democrats did [S12][S6].
After the failed override, the House referred the bill and veto message to Ways and Means, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with no law enacted [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The veto preserved the estate tax and the federal revenue it raised, so general taxpayers were spared the offsetting burden while the heirs of the largest estates kept paying a tax they had come within 16 House votes of eliminating.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax survived

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous at every stage (213 of 222 in the House, 50 of 55 in the Senate, 220 of 223 on override), while most Democrats opposed the bill, though 65 House Democrats and 9 Senate Democrats voted for passage before Democratic unity hardened on the veto override.

industries.note: Only estates above the exemption owed estate tax, so repeal's savings concentrated on the largest estates, with the top rate falling from 55% to zero by 2010. The lost revenue was a cost other taxpayers would have absorbed [S4].

Supporters' central case: rising exemptions and rate cuts would ease estate settlement for family enterprises. But the exemption schedule already shielded most of these estates, and the largest savings went to the biggest estates [S4].
Full repeal would shrink the core estate-tax planning business, though the ten-year phase-out and new carryover basis rules would create years of transition work [S4].
A large market in survivorship insurance exists to cover estate tax liabilities; repeal would gradually eliminate that need.
The estate tax gives large estates a tax reason to leave money to charity; repealing it would remove that incentive, though the bill expanded conservation easement benefits in the interim [S3][S4].
